Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 2 Turn 3 Take Resources 4 Buy Development 5 Activate Production 6 Vatican Report 7 Bonus Action 8 Game End Overview Be the first to reach the end of the faith track OR have 7 development cards Turn On your turn, pick one action: Take Resources Buy Development Activate Production Take Resources Choose a column or row in the market and take all the depicted resources After which, take the spare marble and push it on the row/column you picked to change that row/column If you gain Faith Points, you move your marker on the Faith track rather than gaining resources Place gained resources in your warehouse respecting the following conditions: each depot must contain all of the same resources, and no two depots can store the same resources You have a depot of 1 space, one depot of 2 spaces, and a final depot of 3 storage spaces. When gaining resources, you can move resources around how you like as long as afterwards you keep to the above mentioned conditions If you can't store a resource, it is discarded and all other players gain 1 Faith Point for EACH resource discarded this way Buy Development To buy a development, pay the cost shown in the top middle Development cards need to be bought in level order (levels are displayed via the number of bubbles in the flag) Level 1 cards can be played into your empty spaces Level 2 cards are played over Level 1 cards Level 3 cards are played over Level 2 cards Note only the Level matters when covering up an old card, types don't have to match Activate Production You can activate any and all Development cards previously bought as well as your starting production on your player board (2 same or different resources for 1 resource) ONCE each Any resources gained via Production do NOT go in your Warehouse Depots, instead they are stored in your Strongbox which has no limits on quantity or type All productions are considered to happen at the same time, as such you can't use resources one production would gain you to power another Vatican Report When a player's Faith marker moves over a Pope space, they gain that reward for that section and everyone who has not reached it has to discard theirs, but if you are in the section but not reached the pope you also gain the reward Bonus Action If you wish to discard a leader from your hand, you gain 1 Faith Point If you satisfy the conditions of a leader in your hand, as a bonus action, you can play it to receive an ongoing effect Game End The game ends when a player either reaches the end of the Faith Track or purchases their 7th Development card All Visible and Hidden Development cards score the players points printed on them The Faith Track gives players points based on the nearest passed VP space Any Pope Favour Tiles grant points Played Leader cards grant points For every 5 resources you still have, gain 1VP The player with the most points wins! Take resources from the market and use them to buy new cards. Expand your power both in the city and in the surrounding territories! community_text:
[Rating: 2/10] Being a fan of Lorenzo Il Magnifico is absolutely no reason to even try this "game", let alone own it.  It is a completely tactical randomfest.  Instead of a cube pusher, this is a marble pusher.  You can't plan on collecting the right resources to buy the card that you want, because someone will randomly buy it before you. The resources you get is randomly determined by previous players, so you can't plan at all. There is virtually no strategy in this.  Yet another one-and-done bites the dust.

[Rating: 2/10] Man, I did not like this game.  Right as you build up your engine, the game is over.  Get a better engine going than someone else?  They can just end the game with their 7th discovery card.  It seemed like the 1st player also has a slight advantage, because getting an extra resource can actively screw you over.  And the piles of cards do different things that don't align with others, so if someone takes that card, the next card (with the same color and level) might use a completely different resource and produce something you don't need.  I could go on and on about the reasons I did not like t

[Rating: 2.7/10] Nice mechanic, but no feel of acomplishment. This should be part of a better game, not the entire game... Bored befor the first quarter, waiting for the game to end. Good point for the market management system and being a short game.

[Rating: 3/10] If Splendor and Century Spice Road had a son, this would be it! Altough a little bit more complex than those 2 games, Masters of Renaissence gives you the same feel of engine building, resource management and card drafting! But I have to tell you: Building a successful engine that makes sense in this game is HARD! Super thinkier! That's why it's so easy to just run on the faith track and end the game before anyone makes a good engine. ••• The faith track kills this game for us. It's unbeatable in all our games by a LOT. It has no combos, and almost no engine building at all. A total let down. 

[Rating: 3/10] One play, lovely people. At least it was relatively short, another game just not for me. Probably a bit better at two as you could have half a chance of keeping track of what everyone else is doing but at four I couldn't really care less about the other players. It's a puzzle and if you like puzzles you'll probably like this one but it felt too solitaire for me. Not that I'm big on theme or anything but this didn't make any real sense to me and there was nothing really intuitive about it. I would actively avoid playing it again.

[Rating: 4/10] The resource choosing widget is fantastic – looks good and does its job perfectly.  The cards have a great variety of options, and there is scope for some very interesting engine-building.  The bits are lovely.  And the game is broken. I don’t think the Pope Track strategy is beatable.

[Rating: 4/10] I didn't like this at all - the "engine building" is virtually non existent as you can't use the resources you produce to run other cards in the same turn, so you have to hope you can collect what you need from the gimicky marble device to have a hope of running more than one card a turn, and you probably can't as there's a ridiculous cap on the resources you can store.  Not to mention the limit of 3 cards total.  The game felt arbitrarily restrictive and largely uninteresting.  Takes virtually nothing from Lorenzo other than the look and shouldn't be compared.

[Rating: 4/10] I liked the marble mechanism. What I didn't like is that it's a multiplayer solitaire game and other players maybe grab a card right away that you saved your ressources for. That can be crucial and it's frustrating if it happens multiple times. [Rating: 4/10] This game is a fairly dry euro with simple mechanisms and a gimmicky way of collecting resources.  The lack of any thematic integration doesn't help.  If there was a way to chain combos together when activating your production engine, then I think it would have helped.
